title: Revisiting the status quo bias: Replication of Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988)

source.title: Revisiting the status quo bias: Replication of Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988)
source.authors: Qinyu Xiao, Choi Shan Lam, Muhrajan Piara, and Gilad Feldman

studies.title: Phase 1: budget allocation and wagon color
studies.description: The first U.S. MTurk sample completed two decision scenarios in fixed order.

studies.title: Phase 2: four decision scenarios
studies.description: An independent U.S. MTurk sample repeated the first two scenarios and added investments and college jobs, with randomized scenario order.

nodes.title: Why test status quo framing again?

fields.label: Research question
fields.value: Does presenting a choice as the existing or default option increase its selection, and does the effect differ across scenarios?

fields.label: Motivation
fields.value: The original study suggested an overall bias but a less prominent effect for some options and scenarios. The replication tests whether that variation is repeatable.

fields.label: Status quo versus alternative
fields.value: A given option will be selected more often when framed as the status quo than when framed as an alternative to another status quo option.

fields.label: Status quo versus neutral
fields.value: A given option will be selected more often when framed as the status quo than when no option is designated the status quo.

fields.label: Status quo versus alternative
fields.value: A given option will be selected more often when framed as the status quo than when framed as an alternative to another status quo option.

fields.label: Status quo versus neutral
fields.value: A given option will be selected more often when framed as the status quo than when no option is designated the status quo.

fields.label: Between-participant framing
fields.value: For each scenario, participants were randomly shown one neutral version or one of four versions designating a different option as the status quo. A participant saw only one framing of each scenario.

fields.label: Several choices per participant
fields.value: Each participant completed all scenarios assigned to their phase. Framing varies between participants within a scenario; the scenarios are repeated choices within a participant.

fields.label: Who took part
fields.value: 311 U.S. Mechanical Turk participants completed Phase 1. Mean age 38.05 years (SD 12.38); the paper reports 164 participants as female (52.7%).

fields.label: Who took part
fields.value: 316 U.S. Mechanical Turk participants completed Phase 2. Mean age 38.79 years (SD 11.67); the paper reports 161 participants as female (50.9%).

fields.label: Decision scenarios
fields.value: Choose how to allocate a highway-safety budget between two programs, then choose a color for a wagon. Each scenario presents four alternatives.

fields.label: Decision scenarios
fields.value: Choose a highway-safety budget allocation, a wagon color, an investment portfolio, and a college job. Each scenario presents four alternatives.

fields.label: Administered budget version
fields.value: When 70% auto / 30% highway was the current budget, the survey included a 90% auto / 10% highway choice in place of 50% auto / 50% highway. The authors omitted that version from the 50/50 option’s non-status-quo cell.

fields.label: Per-scenario sequence
fields.value: Participants read the scenario and answered its comprehension questions correctly before seeing the choice options. The status quo versions included a question about which option was current. Choice option display order was randomized.

fields.label: Scenario order
fields.value: Participants encountered the budget scenario and then the wagon scenario.

fields.label: Scenario order
fields.value: The survey presented the four scenarios in randomized order.

fields.label: Manipulated variable
fields.value: Within each scenario, the version either designates one of the four options as the status quo or presents all options without a status quo.

fields.label: Outcome
fields.value: One choice per scenario. For each candidate option the analysis compares the proportion of participants who selected it under each framing.

nodes.title: Compare choice rates for the same option

fields.label: Main comparisons
fields.value: The authors used independent-proportions tests for each option, comparing the status quo framing with the pooled alternative framings and separately with the neutral framing. Results include chi-square tests, odds ratios, and Cohen’s h.

fields.label: Exclusion check
fields.value: The main text reports full-sample analyses and the supplement repeats them after preregistered exclusions. The authors report no major discrepancies overall and separately document the Phase 2 budget wording error.

fields.label: Comparison with the 1988 study
fields.value: The authors evaluated effect signal and consistency with original effects using the LeBel criteria. This comparison uses results from the original sample as a historical reference.

fields.label: Published human result
fields.value: All four options were chosen significantly more as status quo than as alternatives (p ≤ .002). Three of four also exceeded the neutral rate significantly. The 30% auto / 70% highway comparison with neutral was inconclusive (p = .294, OR 1.46, 95% CI 0.72–2.97).

fields.label: Published human result
fields.value: No status quo versus alternative test showed a significant advantage. White was the only significant status quo versus neutral comparison (p = .024, OR 2.81, 95% CI 1.12–7.07).

fields.label: Which test was significant?
fields.value: The Discussion describes the white result as status quo versus alternative. The Results and Tables 1–2 put the significant result in the neutral comparison. The alternative comparison has p = .110.
fields.derivation: Compared the contrast-specific p-values in Tables 1–2 with the descriptions in Results and Discussion.

fields.label: Published human result
fields.value: All four status quo versus alternative tests were significant (p ≤ .001), as were three status quo versus neutral tests (p ≤ .026). The 50% auto / 50% highway neutral comparison was inconclusive (p = .104, OR 1.79, 95% CI 0.88–3.64).

fields.label: Affected comparison
fields.value: The 50/50 option had one fewer alternative framing because the corresponding administered survey version offered 90/10 instead.

fields.label: Published human result
fields.value: Red and tan showed higher choice rates as status quo than as alternatives by the reported tests. The tan chi-square test had p = .048, and its reported odds-ratio interval includes 1. Silver blue was chosen less often as status quo than as an alternative. None of the neutral comparisons was significant.

fields.label: Published human result
fields.value: The reported odds ratios favored the status quo for all options. Tests for the Moderate Risk and High Risk options were inconclusive against either reference.

fields.label: Scenario number in the Results
fields.value: The Results paragraph names Scenario 2 for these options, while Tables 3–4 place them in the investment scenario (Scenario 3).
fields.derivation: Matched the two named options to the scenario heading of their table rows.

nodes.title: Phase 2 college jobs: support varies by option

fields.label: Published human result
fields.value: College C was the only option across the investment and college scenarios significant against both references. The College D choice rates did not follow the predicted ordering of status quo highest and alternative lowest.

nodes.title: Framing effects depend on the scenario

fields.label: Paper’s conclusion
fields.value: Budget allocation, investment portfolios and college jobs showed evidence of status quo framing overall. Wagon color showed weak or limited support in both phases and differed most from the original results.

fields.label: Hypothetical choices
fields.value: The survey tests how a designated status quo affects hypothetical choices. Participants did not make the prior choice described in the scenario.

fields.label: Mechanisms remain untested
fields.value: The authors discuss why wagon color could produce a weaker bias, including lower switching costs and less personal attachment. The study did not manipulate these mechanisms.

fields.label: Original study coverage
fields.value: The replication covers a subset of the original four-option scenarios and leaves out scenarios with other option counts and sequential choices.

fields.label: Precision
fields.value: The authors’ revised post hoc calculation suggested 355 participants for 95% power at a medium effect. Neither phase reached that number.

evidence.quote: Status quo bias refers to people’s general preference to stick to, or continue with, a previously chosen option.

We hence aimed to revisit this classic phenomenon to examine the replicability of the original findings with independent replications. Although Samuelson and Zeckhauser’s (1988) results supported a status quo bias overall, the bias seemed to be less prominent for some options and in some of their decision-making scenarios than in others.

The current replications focused on Questions 1, 2, 4, and 6 in Part One of Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988) and had two phases. The first-phase replication focused on Questions 1 and 6, and the second-
phase replication focused on all four questions.

A total of 311 (Mage = 38.05, SD = 12.38; 164 (52.7%) females) and 316 (Mage = 38.79, SD = 11.67; 161 (50.9%) females) Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) participants completed the first and the second phases of our replications, respectively.

In two pre-registered experiments with U.S. participants recruited from the Amazon Mechanical Turk (n1 = 311, n2 = 316), we attempted to replicate four decision scenarios (Question 1, 2, 4, and 6) from Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988), the seminal article that provided the first experimental demonstration of the status quo bias.
The order of presentation was fixed in the first phase but randomized in the second phase (there was no sign that this variation had any major influence on the results).

budget allocation ratios for safety research programs, (2) color options for a wagon that one just purchased, (3) investment portfolios, and (4) college job offers. Each question had four options. Participants in the first-phase replication answered Scenario 1 and 2 only, whereas those in the second phase answered all four scenarios.

Each Scenario was presented in one out of five versions: one neutral version and four status quo versions. In the neutral version, no option was the status quo. In the status quo versions, one of the four options was framed as the status quo, i.e., as a previously chosen or the default option. Participants were randomly presented with only one version for each scenario.

The display order of the options was randomized. All scenario descriptions were followed by a few comprehension questions to ensure that participants read and understood the texts. Particularly, for the status quo versions, participants were additionally asked what the status quo was. They had to answer these comprehension questions correctly before proceeding to see the options and make their choices.
Participants saw any option under only one framing, in accordance with the between-subjects design of the experiments.

The target study used two-option, three-option, as well as four-option versions for the decision questions. We used only the four-option versions in our replications due to online survey administration time constraints, and for simplifying the design without looking into the number of options as a possible moderating factor.

We pre-registered our power analyses and reported that we aimed at 300 participants in the pre-registrations. Nevertheless, as one reviewer pointed out, those power analyses were inadequate. Therefore, we conducted an additional “post hoc” (i.e., after data collection) power analysis, which suggested that we would need 355 participants in order to detect a Cohen’s medium effect at .95 power with the planned tests. Although we did not meet this number, our sample sizes were close to it, and hence our replications may still be considered to have adequate power.

We reported the full sample results here in the main text. For the results after exclusion, please refer to Table 8S to 11S in the supplementary. There were no major discrepancies between these results. Apart from excluding based on the pre-registered criteria, we additionally excluded part of the data as after data collection, we found an error in the questionnaire used in the second-phase replication (please refer to the supplementary for details).
Independent-proportions tests were conducted to compare the choice rates between the status quo and non-status quo framing, and between the status quo and the neutral framing.

As noted in the beginning, we summarized our replications as very close replications using the criteria set by LeBel et al. (2018). We aimed to compare the replication effects with the original effects using the criteria set by LeBel et al. (2019) (Figure 1S).

The options in Scenario 1 had significantly higher choice rates as the status quo than as a non-status quo, χ2 ≥ 9.38, ps ≤ .002, smallest odds ratio = 2.47, 95% CI [1.37, 4.44], smallest Cohen’s h = 0.44, 95% CI [0.16, 0.73]. The effects were of medium sizes (0.5) by Cohen’s (1988) benchmarks. Comparing the choice rates of options under the status quo framing and the neutral framing, we found, however, one non-significant difference (for the option “30A70H”), χ2 = 1.10, p = .294, odds ratio = 1.46, 95% CI [0.72, 2.97], Cohen’s h = 0.19, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.54]. The other three differences were statistically significant, ps ≤ .033. The effect sizes ranged from 2.16 to 4.83 in odds ratio or 0.38 to 0.57 in Cohen’s h. Overall, our data provided strong support for the status quo bias (both H1 and H2) in Scenario 1.

We found weak-to-no support for the status quo bias, or H1 and H2, in Scenario 2. Comparing the status quo framing with the non-status quo framing, we observed no significant differences in the expected direction, χ2 ≤ 2.56, ps ≥ .110. Comparing the status quo framing with the neutral framing, only one option (white color) had a significant and small-to-medium difference in the expected direction, χ2 = 5.06, p = .024, odds ratio = 2.81, 95% CI [1.12, 7.07], Cohen’s h = 0.41, 95% CI [0.06, 0.76].

We observed the hypothesized pattern (i.e., the choice rate of an option is the highest under the status quo framing and the lowest under the non-status quo framing) in 12 out of the 16 options from the four scenarios (the exceptions were: “30A70H” in Scenario 1; silver blue and white in Scenario 2; and College D in Scenario 4).

Again, we conducted independent-proportions test to examine H1 and H2. The status quo framing resulted in significantly higher choice rates for nearly all options from Scenario 1, regardless of whether it was compared against the non-status quo framing (χ2 ≥ 10.81, ps ≤ .001, lowest odds ratio = 2.78, 95% CI [1.49, 5.17], lowest Cohen’s h = 0.46, 95% CI [0.17, 0.74]) or against the neutral framing (for those significant differences: χ2 ≥ 4.97, ps ≤ .026, lowest odds ratio = 2.40, 95% CI [1.10, 5.21], lowest Cohen’s h = 0.40, 95% CI [0.05, 0.74]). The only exception was the “50A50H” option, for which the comparison between the status quo framing and the neutral framing did not result in a significant difference, χ2 = 2.64, p = .104; though the effect was in the predicted direction, odds ratio = 1.79, 95% CI [0.88, 3.64], Cohen’s h = 0.29, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.64].

Although most options from Scenario 3 and 4 exhibited the hypothesized pattern, the results of our independent-proportions tests did not consistently meet the criterion for statistical significance. There was only one option (College C in Scenario 4) for which both comparisons (i.e., status quo vs. non-
status quo and status quo vs. neutral) yielded statistically significant differences. There were two options (Moderate Risk and High Risk in Scenario 2) for which both differences were not significant. Comparing the status quo framing with the non-status quo framing, the effect sizes ranged from 1.66 to 3.15 in odds ratio or 0.16 to 0.47 in Cohen’s h in Scenario 3, and from 1.81 to 4.88 in odds ratio or 0.27 to 0.75 in Cohen’s h in Scenario 4. Comparing the status quo framing with the neutral framing, the effect sizes ranged from 1.31 to 1.85 in odds ratio or 0.09 to 0.31 in Cohen’s h in Scenario 3, and from 1.75 to 3.26 in odds ratio or 0.23 to 0.58 in Cohen’s h in Scenario 4. Despite those non-significant differences, our data still provide good support overall for the status quo bias in these two scenarios. The bias seemed to be more pronounced in Scenario 4 than in 3 based on the observed effect sizes.

Like in the first-phase replication, we found the least support for the status quo bias in Scenario 2. Two options from this scenario did not exhibit the hypothesized pattern. For silver blue, the non-status quo framing even led to higher choice rate than the

status quo framing. Comparing the status quo framing with the non-status quo framing, we observed significant differences for two options (for the tan color: odds ratio = 2.33, 95% CI [0.99, 5.51], Cohen’s h = 0.27, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.56]; for the red color: odds ratio = 3.11, 95% CI [1.56, 6.20], Cohen’s h = 0.46, 95% CI [0.17, 0.74]). Comparing the status quo framing with the neutral framing, all differences were non-
significant, with the option of tan color exhibiting the largest effect size (odds ratio = 2.00, 95% CI [0.68, 5.89], Cohen’s h = 0.23, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.58]). Overall, our data provided limited support for the status quo bias in Scenario 2.

Scenario 2 results, however, had the largest discrepancy when compared with the original results. The original study observed two significant differences when the status quo framing was compared with the neutral framing, whereas in our replications, only the white color option in the first-
phase replication had a significant difference in the status quo vs. non-status quo comparison. Moreover, we had three comparisons that yielded effects in the opposite direction (red and silver blue in the first phase and white in the second phase). Overall, our replication findings for Scenario 2 deviated the most from the original.

We conducted two phases of pre-registered replications of the status quo bias, focusing on four hypothetical decision scenarios from Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988). Our results were mostly consistent with the original findings. We found support for the status quo bias in three scenarios but weak-
to-no support in the remaining one (i.e., Scenario 2).
We were limited by our inability to experimentally control or manipulate the factors that we discussed above, since we aimed primarily at direct replications.

To be precise, what we attempted to replicate was the effect of status quo framing, since our experiments did not involve participants’ actual previous choices. Therefore, more evidence is needed if our findings are to be generalized to situations where actual previous choices serve as the status quo.
Still, we did not attempt to replicate the original experiment in full, leaving out some original scenarios and using only the four-option versions.

issues.title: Phase 1 Word export does not record runtime settings
issues.reason: The fielded Word survey shows two scenarios and omits Qualtrics runtime settings. The available editable Qualtrics export describes four scenarios.
issues.impact: The Phase 1 Word export does not confirm the exact settings used in the field.
issues.suggestedAction: A Qualtrics export of the actual two-scenario fielded survey would resolve this gap.

issues.title: White wagon contrast differs in the Results and Discussion
issues.reason: The Phase 1 white result is attributed to the alternative comparison in the Discussion but to the neutral comparison in the Results and Tables 1–2.
issues.impact: The paper’s Discussion can lead a reader to report a different comparison as significant.
issues.suggestedAction: Use the original table for the particular comparison being reported.

issues.title: One Phase 2 budget framing has a different option
issues.reason: The administered 70/30 status quo version offered a 90/10 option in place of 50/50.
issues.impact: The authors excluded that version from the 50/50 option’s alternative-framing denominator.
issues.suggestedAction: Preserve the fielded wording and the documented denominator when reproducing that contrast.

issues.title: Investment options are misnumbered in the Results prose
issues.reason: The paper calls Moderate Risk and High Risk Scenario 2 options in one sentence. Tables 3 and 4 place both options in Scenario 3.
issues.impact: A reader following that sentence alone could assign the two results to the wagon scenario.
issues.suggestedAction: Use the investment table rows to identify the results.
